summary.text: 工 is a whole-graph pictograph proposed to depict a tool, though its precise object is disputed. Today it means work or labor; early records also use it for occupations, but the evidence does not establish a clear sequence linking these meanings.

formation.text: Pictographic: early forms are interpreted as a tool, with proposals including a carpenter’s square, but the precise object is disputed. 工 is treated as one pictured graph, not a combination of internal parts. A separate transmitted historical account glosses it as 巧飾, skilled finishing, and explains the shape as a person possessing 規榘; this is a distinct interpretation, not confirmation of a particular tool.

components.text: 工 is treated as one complete pictorial graph, proposed to depict a tool. Its exact referent is disputed; no separate internal components are identified.

history.text: Labeled oracle-script and small-seal renderings show historical forms of 工. Early graphs are interpreted as tools, but the proposed object remains disputed. A separate account proposes that lower strokes changed from thicker forms to a thin horizontal; that graphic account does not settle the pictured object.
A transmitted historical account records 𢒄, which includes 彡, as an ancient form of 工. It does not specify whether that graph is an ancestor, a variant, or another kind of related form.

uncertainties.text: The proposed object is disputed, and its spoken name and pronunciation are not established. 工’s reconstructed readings do not identify the object. The cited early artifacts are not dated in the accounts, so they do not establish the earliest attestation of each use.

It is unclear whether early official or status uses relate to craft and work, or whether these meanings form a chronological chain. 工 is also reported as a whole-graph loan for 貢 in oracle-bone contexts; the sound comparison and dates are not established here.

senses.gloss: proposed tool referent of the graph
senses.text: The graph is interpreted as picturing a tool, with proposals including a carpenter’s square. The precise object remains disputed, and the cited accounts do not date the relevant artifacts. This is a proposal about the pictured graph, not an independently established word use or earliest attestation.
Reported oracle-bone examples use 工 as a state or place name. This use is not connected to the proposed tool meaning.

senses.gloss: official title, status, or occupation term
senses.period: early oracle-bone and bronze examples; dating unresolved
senses.text: Reported early examples use 工 for status or occupation, including craft-related uses. A bronze inscription is reported to use it in an official title interpreted as 司空. The relationship between title/status and craft-worker uses is unresolved.
工 is currently used for a worker, as in 木工 and 矿工. These examples support present-day usage; earlier craft-worker and skilled-maker attestations are discussed separately.
工 currently means work or labor. The evidence does not give a dated sequence showing how this use developed from the proposed tool or craft-worker senses.

senses.gloss: achievement, written with 工 for 功
senses.period: bronze inscriptions and Warring States bamboo slip; artifact dates unresolved here
senses.text: In cited bronze-inscription and Warring States-slip contexts, 工 is read as 功, ‘achievement’. This is graphic interchange or borrowing in those contexts, not proof that 工’s work sense developed into achievement.

senses.gloss: tribute or offering, written with 工 for 貢
senses.text: In reported oracle-bone contexts, 工 writes 貢. This proposed whole-graph loan means the sign was reused for another word because the words were said to sound alike or similarly, not because the tool meaning changed into ‘tribute’. The early sound match is not independently established by the cited account.

limitations.text: The cited artifact examples are not individually dated in these accounts, so they do not establish the earliest attestation of each use. Glosses and listed meanings alone do not demonstrate a chronological semantic chain.

The proposed tool referent, the relationship between early official or status uses and craft or work uses, and the sound basis of the 貢 loan remain unresolved. Close reconstructed readings for 工, 功, and 攻 do not establish a shared semantic history.
